client: I've been really stressed out lately because I got a lower grade than I expected on my last exam, and now I can't stop thinking about how it might ruin my GPA. It feels like everything I've worked for is just falling apart, and I keep replaying the exam in my head wondering what I did wrong. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the grade is already there and nothing can fix it now.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a lot of weight right now — that loop of replaying the exam and fearing what it means for your future is exhausting, and it makes sense you're feeling overwhelmed. I also notice you mentioned that talking might not help, and I'm curious about that thought — do you find yourself sometimes dismissing support before giving it a chance, almost as a way of protecting yourself from more disappointment? Let's gently explore what's underneath that belief, because how we interpret a setback often shapes how much power it has over us.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Maybe you're right that I push support away before really trying it, but I think it's more that I've talked to people about stress before and it never actually changed anything concrete. Like, my friend told me "one grade doesn't define you" and I know that's probably true on some level, but it didn't make the anxiety go away. I guess I'm just skeptical that exploring my feelings about it will do anything when the actual problem is the number sitting on my transcript.
therapist: Your skepticism makes a lot of sense — being told "one grade doesn't define you" can feel hollow when the anxiety is still very much there, and you're right that talking doesn't erase the grade. What CBT can actually help with, though, isn't changing the number but loosening the grip of the story you're telling yourself about what that number *means* — because right now it sounds like part of you has decided it means everything is falling apart, and that belief is what's fueling the spiral. Does that distinction feel worth exploring a little?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess that distinction makes some sense, but I'm not sure I'm telling myself a "story" so much as just... responding to reality. Like, my GPA actually does matter for grad school applications, so it's not completely irrational to be worried about it. I'm willing to explore it a little, but I'm nervous it's going to feel like I'm just being talked into pretending things are fine when they're not.
therapist: You're absolutely right that your GPA matters, and the goal here isn't to talk you into pretending everything is fine — that would just be a different kind of unhelpful story. The distinction CBT tries to make is between *accurate* concern ("this grade affects my GPA") and *amplified* thinking ("this means everything I've worked for is falling apart") — and it sounds like right now those two things might be blending together in a way that's making the anxiety much harder to carry. Would you be open to looking at what the evidence actually says about where things stand, rather than where your most anxious thoughts say they stand?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Okay, I can try that, though I'm a little worried that looking at the evidence is just going to confirm my fears rather than ease them. Like, what if I do the math and my GPA actually has dropped significantly — doesn't that just make things worse? I guess what I'm saying is that part of me would almost rather not know exactly how bad it is, because right now at least it's just a vague worry and not a confirmed disaster.
therapist: That instinct to avoid confirming the fear is really human — there's a kind of fragile safety in uncertainty, because a vague worry at least leaves room for hope. But I'm curious: do you notice how much energy it's already taking to carry this *without* knowing, replaying the exam, imagining worst cases? Sometimes the confirmed reality, even if difficult, is actually easier to work with than the anxious unknown our minds tend to make even bigger than it is.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, fast speech

client: Yeah, I do notice that — I've barely been able to focus on anything else this week, so I guess the avoidance isn't exactly working. It's just that there's a difference between knowing something might be bad and having it confirmed, because once it's confirmed it feels more real and harder to dismiss. But I hear what you're saying, and maybe sitting with the uncertainty is actually costing me more than just... looking at the numbers would.
therapist: It sounds like something just shifted a little for you — recognizing that the avoidance is costing you is actually a meaningful insight, and it takes courage to sit with that honestly. I notice you're speaking quite softly right now, and I wonder if underneath the logic there's still something tender about taking that step toward the numbers — like it's not just information, but a moment of facing yourself. What do you think you'd need to feel okay enough to actually look?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think what makes it feel like "facing myself" is that I've always tied my self-worth pretty closely to my academic performance, so a bad grade doesn't just feel like a setback, it feels like proof that I'm not as capable as I thought I was. To actually look at the numbers, I think I'd need to remind myself beforehand that whatever I see doesn't change who I am — but honestly, I'm not sure I fully believe that yet. It's easy to say it but harder to actually feel it when you're in the middle of it.
therapist: What you just named — that a grade feels like *proof* about your worth rather than just feedback about one performance — is really at the heart of what's been making this so painful, and it's a pattern that CBT can genuinely help untangle. It's okay that you don't fully believe yet that your worth is separate from your performance; belief usually follows *experience*, not the other way around, so we'd work on building small moments that start to show you that's true. What's one area of your life, even a small one, where you feel capable or valued that has nothing to do with grades?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I guess... I'm actually a pretty good listener when my friends come to me with problems, and a few people have told me they feel like I really get them in a way others don't. But it's hard to hold onto that right now because it feels kind of small compared to something like a GPA, which has these concrete long-term consequences. I don't know, maybe I'm just dismissing it too quickly, but it doesn't feel like the same kind of thing.
therapist: You actually caught yourself in the middle of dismissing it — "maybe I'm just dismissing it too quickly" — which shows a part of you recognizes that being someone people genuinely feel understood by is *not* a small thing, even if it's hard to feel that right now. It's worth noticing that your GPA feels big because it's measurable and has a label, but the qualities that make you a good friend — empathy, presence, the ability to really *get* someone — those shape your life and relationships in ways a transcript never could. What do you think it would take to let that kind of evidence count just as much?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think part of the problem is that nobody ever really rewarded me for being a good listener — like, there's no grade for that, no external validation that tells me I'm doing well. So even if I intellectually accept that it matters, I don't have the same kind of reinforcement loop that I have with academics, where someone literally gives you a number that says "yes, you did this right." I'm not sure how to start valuing something that the world around me doesn't seem to measure or reward in the same way.
therapist: You've just named something really important — that you've essentially been trained to trust external measurements over internal ones, so anything that doesn't come with a score feels somehow less real or less earned. And yet, the fact that your friends *seek you out*, that they feel genuinely understood by you, is its own kind of feedback — it's just quieter than a grade, and it sounds like somewhere along the way you learned to turn the volume down on that kind of signal. I'm curious, when a friend tells you that you really got them — what happens inside you in that moment, before the part of you that dismisses it kicks in?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: Honestly, in that first moment before I brush it off, there's this brief warmth — like a small relief that I actually did something right, that I mattered to someone in that moment. But it fades really quickly, almost like I don't trust it to last or like it doesn't count as real evidence of anything. I think I've gotten so used to needing something permanent and documented that a feeling, even a good one, just doesn't feel like enough proof.
therapist: That brief warmth you described — that's not nothing, that's actually your real self responding before the critic steps in and takes the microphone away. It's striking that you called it "relief," like mattering to someone is something you've been quietly waiting for permission to feel. What would it be like to practice just... staying with that warmth a little longer next time, before the part of you that needs documentation rushes in to dismiss it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I like the idea of staying with that warmth longer, but I'm honestly not sure I'll remember to do it in the moment — it happens so fast and then it's gone before I even realize I dismissed it. It's also a little uncomfortable to sit with good feelings sometimes, almost like if I let myself feel too good about something it'll get taken away or I'll jinx it somehow. I guess that's kind of strange to admit, but it feels true.
therapist: It's not strange at all — what you're describing is actually really common, this sense that good feelings are fragile or borrowed, like happiness has a catch. That belief that joy might be "taken away" if you lean into it too fully is worth gently examining, because it might be quietly keeping you at arm's length from your own life. Where do you think that feeling first came from — was there a time when letting yourself feel good about something did lead to disappointment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
